News
Vidi grant for George Kelesidis
The Dutch Research Council NWO has awarded no fewer than thirteen promising scientists from TU Delft a Vidi grant. One of them is George Kelesidis, Assistant Professor of Flight Performance and Propulsion. With the Vidi grant of up to €850,000, Kelesidis can further develop his own line of research into cleaner aircraft engines and expand his own research group. The aim of George Kelesidis’ research is to reduce the environmental and health impacts of aviation emissions.
The science behind world’s fastest autonomous racing drone
Researchers at Delft University of Technology (The Netherlands) have developed an AI system that enables a racing drone to navigate demanding courses at extreme speed using only a single camera. It outperformed even former world champion human drone-pilots in a race.
TU Delft appoints Robert van Tilborg as Professor of Practice
Per 1 October 2026, TU Delft has appointed Robert van Tilborg as Professor of Practice at the Faculty of Aerospace Engineering – a role designed to help the university align its research agenda more closely with industry and bring the university’s emerging technology and innovations to market faster. The university announced the news at the Aerospace Innovation Hub's DEMOday.
BSc Aerospace Engineering: new bilingual track (NL/EN) alongside the English track
From October 2026, prospective students wishing to apply for the bachelor’s programme in Aerospace Engineering will be able to choose between two tracks: a track with an English-language selection process and fully English-language teaching, as is currently the case, and a track with a partially Dutch-language selection process and partially Dutch-language teaching in the first year.
Jeroen Wink Named TU Delft Alumnus of the Year 2026
Alumnus Jeroen Wink, co-founder and Chief Revenue Officer of Dawn Aerospace. Through his pioneering work in sustainable space technology and his role in building a globally recognised aerospace company, Wink is helping to create a future in which spaceflight becomes more accessible, sustainable, and economically viable.
The Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets have lost over 11 trillion tonnes of ice since 1979
Three scientists from Delft are taking part in the global research collaboration involving polar researchers: Pavel Ditmar, Ernst Schrama and Bert Wouters contributed to determining the total mass loss of Greenland and Antarctica using satellite data. On 16 September, the consortium published the research findings in the Nature journal Scientific Data.
Bio-inspired whiskers enable tiny drones to navigate in darkness using touch
Tiny autonomous drones could soon navigate through darkness, dust and smoke using artificial whiskers inspired by animals. Their small size limits the use of large or heavy sensors for navigation. That's why researchers from TU Delft have developed a lightweight whisker-based tactile sensor that enables drones to navigate and explore their surroundings through gentle touch. The study was recently published in Nature Communications.
From lab to space: TU Delft-led mission to test photonic chip in orbit
The Netherlands is a leader in both photonic chips and space technology. Now these two worlds meet, as two teams at TU Delft’s Faculty of Aerospace Engineering are joining forces. One develops miniature satellites, the other uses advanced photonic chips to search for signs of life. Together, they will bring a photonic sensing system from the lab to a TU Delft-built satellite.
Drones navigating by touch: ERC Starting Grant for Salua Hamaza
Dr. Salua Hamaza, Associate Professor Aerial Physical Interaction & Embodied Intelligence in Aerial robots, has been awarded an ERC Starting Grant of €1.62 million to develop a game changer. She will pioneer tactile perception as a new sensing modality for autonomous flight, allowing drones to use touch for navigation in a five-year research programme.

Stories of Aerospace Engineering
Cardiologist applies aviation models to healthcare
Modern aircraft automatically remain within their safety limits whilst in flight. The boundaries of an aircraft’s safe ‘flight envelope’ are continuously calculated using complex and changing data on factors such as the aircraft’s current speed, altitude, load and weight. Cardiologist and intensivist Christiaan Meuwese of Erasmus MC drew inspiration from aviation safety models. Together with aviation expert Joris Melkert of Delft University of Technology, he developed a new concept to calculate personal safety margins for patients as well.
Looking beyond the end of the wind turbine blade
The tips of wind turbine blades sometimes rotate at speeds of several hundred kilometres per hour. At such high speeds, precipitation can cause considerable damage to the coating of a blade, resulting in loss of energy production. Using rain experiments, Structures and Materials researcher Julie Teuwen mapped out the impact of precipitation on wind turbine blades.
Open Your Ears: Building a sounder future through open science
Noise pollution is one of the most pressing environmental health challenges across Europe. Often overlooked in the design of modern products and infrastructure, sound plays a vital role in both human well-being and technological progress. In response to this need, Open Your Ears, a collaborative project at TU Delft led by Assistant Professor Roberto Merino Martinez, is developing open-source tools to transform the way we assess and design sound—making it more accessible, realistic, and meaningful.
Using quantum technology to find the strongest and lightest composite for aeroplanes
How do you find the most optimal combination when there are countless options? Using a quantum algorithm, Associate Professor Boyang Chen is searching for the best stacking sequence of fibres in composites to create the lightest and strongest material for aircraft. The QAIMS Lab that Chen founded at TU Delft, is the first research team in the world to use quantum computing for this application. In the coming years, Chen hopes to work with aircraft manufacturer Airbus to discover the possibilities of the quantum algorithm for the industry: how much profit can be made from it and of course how can it contribute to cleaner aviation?
The world of gas dynamics turned upside down
It’s 1942, and astrophysicist Hans Bethe, who would later win the Nobel Prize, describes a revolutionary theory. If correct, it will overturn some of the principles of gas dynamics. However, it would take more than 80 years for this to happen. It wasn’t until 2024 that thermodynamicist Piero Colonna and his team at TU Delft found proof of non-classical gas dynamics. ‘As a researcher, you need to give yourself the freedom to pursue your curiosity.’
Discover how Delft’s start-up Dawn Aerospace is revolutionizing spaceflight by creating reusable rockets and eco-friendly propulsion systems. Co-founder Jeroen Wink shares insights on their journey from a student project to a global player, and discusses how Europe can enhance its strategic position in space technology.
Delft’s rocket dreamers building reusable spaceflight
Discover how Delft’s start-up Dawn Aerospace is revolutionizing spaceflight by creating reusable rockets and eco-friendly propulsion systems. Co-founder Jeroen Wink shares insights on their journey from a student project to a global player, and discusses how Europe can enhance its strategic position in space technology.
Supercomputer helps to decrease sound pollution: turn that noise down!
Together with his team of researchers in Delft, Frits de Prenter studies the sound caused by airflows when they come into contact with objects. This research, which requires considerable computing power, is contributing to the development of quieter aircraft, drones, and wind turbines.
A new air traffic puzzle: autonomous drones in the sky
Fast package deliveries to your doorstep, providing medical aid to remote areas, or monitoring large crowds from above—these are all potential applications for autonomous drones. But can this be done safely? Joost Ellerbroek, Assistant Professor of Control & Operations at the Faculty of Aerospace Engineering, is exploring how to design Unmanned Traffic Management (UTM). He is working on developing smart algorithms to ensure autonomous drones fly optimal routes without colliding.
The ground truth: airport operations for hydrogen-powered aviation
It is not only aircraft that must be prepared for flying on hydrogen, ground operations at the airport need to run very smoothly too. Quite a challenge when considering the fuelling, space, and safety requirements. The models and simulations developed by Alexei Sharpanskykh, Assistant Professor Operations & Environment, help shape this future.
Mastering fuel flow in hydrogen-powered airplanes
Airplanes powered by liquid hydrogen are expected to play a key role in creating low-emission aviation. But once safely stored on board, an even greater challenge is to control the hydrogen flow and have it reach the engines at the required temperature and pressure. Chiara Falsetti, Assistant Professor in Heat Transfer and Thermal Management for Sustainable Aviation, wants to fully understand how hydrogen flows through airplane fuel pipes.
Cracking and tracking – ultrasonics for hydrogen-powered aviation
Monitoring and ensuring the safety of hydrogen storage tanks over tens of thousands of airplane refuellings presents a unique challenge on the road towards low-emission aviation. Nan Yue, Assistant Professor in the Aerospace Structures and Materials Department, develops ultrasonic technology for detecting the very early signs of cracks appearing in the tank hull.
Flame on for hydrogen-powered aircraft propulsion
Flying on hydrogen eliminates CO2 emissions but comes with challenges in flame stability, NOx emissions and reliability, especially given the strict aviation standards. Francesca De Domenico, Assistant Professor in Sustainable Aircraft Propulsion, sees this as an opportunity to radically re-think and innovate combustion systems for aviation. Her experimental research lays the groundwork for addressing these issues and advancing sustainable flight.
